beats.intro: Derivatives, module three. [[sub]]Why people use derivatives, what can go wrong, and how issuers and investors use them differently.
beats.benefits: [[a]]Derivatives bridge a timing gap. A manufacturer must order materials before it receives orders. An investor decides today, but will only receive cash later. A derivative lets them act now at a price agreed in advance. [[b1]]First benefit: risk can be allocated, transferred and managed without trading the underlying, and exposures can be created that the cash market cannot offer. [[b2]]Second: information. Futures prices hint at where cash markets are heading, and option prices reveal expected volatility. [[b3]]Third: operational advantages. A smaller cash outlay, lower transaction costs, more liquidity, and easy short positions. [[b4]]Fourth: market efficiency. Exploiting a mispricing is cheaper, so prices adjust faster.
beats.hedge: [[a]]Montau, a German machine maker, will receive six hundred fifty million Korean won in seventy-five days. Its costs are in euros. [[unh]]If it does nothing, its profit margin moves with the exchange rate. When the won is weak, at fifteen twenty-five per euro, the margin is about negative one percent. When the won is strong, at twelve twenty-five, it is nineteen percent. [[fwd]]Instead, Montau sells the won forward, at thirteen fifty. That locks in four hundred eighty-one thousand euros, and an eleven percent margin, whatever the exchange rate does. [[pt]]The forward offsets the exposure. That is a hedge.
beats.outlay: [[a]]Back to Procam and its gold. Buying one hundred ounces in the spot market costs one hundred seventy-seven thousand dollars. [[fut]]Gaining the same exposure with a futures contract needs only forty-nine fifty of initial margin. [[int]]Financed at five percent for three months, the spot purchase costs about twenty-two hundred in interest. The futures margin costs about sixty-two dollars. [[note]]Spot gold would also need delivery, storage and insurance. Futures need none of that.
beats.leverage: [[a]]The same feature is also a risk. Low outlay means implicit leverage. [[end]]In three months, gold ends at seventeen eighty fifty, so both positions are worth one hundred seventy-eight thousand fifty. [[own]]On the cash outlay, the spot buyer gains point five nine percent. The futures buyer, who agreed to pay one hundred seventy-nine thousand two hundred thirteen, loses twenty-three point five percent of the margin. [[bor]]If everything is borrowed, the spot gain is forty-seven point five percent of the interest cost, but the futures loss is eighteen hundred seventy-nine percent. [[pt]]Leverage magnifies returns and risks, and it explains why derivative losses can be so severe.
beats.covered: [[a]]Derivatives can also create profiles that cash markets do not offer. Take an investor who owns an index, and expects it to end flat or slightly higher. [[sell]]It sells a call option with a strike above the current price, and collects the premium. This is called a covered call. [[lo]]If the index rises less than the strike, the call expires, and the investor keeps the premium on top of the gain. [[hi]]If it rises beyond the strike, the investor gives up the extra gain. The premium is kept either way.
beats.risks: [[a]]Derivatives also bring risks. [[r1]]Speculative use: high implicit leverage can lead to financial distress. [[r2]]Lack of transparency: complex positions may not be understood. [[r3]]Basis risk: the derivative's value drifts away from the exposure it hedges. [[r4]]Liquidity risk: cash flows arrive at different times, for example a margin call you cannot fund. [[r5]]Counterparty credit risk: the other side may not pay. [[r6]]And systemic risk: excessive leverage can destabilize markets, as in two thousand eight.
beats.credit: [[a]]Credit exposure depends on the contract. [[opt]]With a call option, only the buyer is exposed. Once the seller has received the premium, it has no credit risk to the buyer. The buyer depends on the seller to pay if the option finishes in the money. [[fwd]]With a forward, both sides are exposed, because either could owe money at maturity. [[etd]]On exchanges, daily settlement and margin keep this exposure small. [[otc]]In the OTC market, credit terms vary, from no collateral at all to margining like futures. [[ccp]]Central clearing standardizes margin and reduces counterparty risk.
beats.issuers: [[a]]Issuers mainly use derivatives to hedge market exposures that come with running a business. [[acc]]Derivatives are recorded at fair value, and gains and losses go through earnings, unless hedge accounting applies. Hedge accounting offsets the derivative against what it hedges, to reduce volatility in the statements. [[cf]]A cash flow hedge covers variable cash flows. Montau's forward is one, and so is a swap that fixes the rate on floating-rate debt. [[fv]]A fair value hedge covers changes in the value of an asset or liability, such as swapping a fixed-rate bond into floating. [[ni]]A net investment hedge covers the currency risk of a foreign operation.
beats.investors: [[a]]Investors use derivatives differently. [[u1]]To replicate a cash market strategy more cheaply, since derivatives need less capital and are more liquid. [[u2]]To hedge, for example removing currency risk from an overseas investment. [[u3]]To modify or add exposure: shorts, extra duration, or option profiles. [[nav]]Investors worry less about hedge accounting, because a fund's derivatives are marked to market daily in its net asset value. They also trade more often on exchanges. [[pro]]A fund's prospectus states which derivatives it may use, and why.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Derivatives allocate risk, reveal information, cut costs and improve market efficiency. [[w2]]Implicit leverage magnifies gains and losses, and there are basis, liquidity, counterparty and systemic risks. [[w3]]Issuers mostly hedge, and seek hedge accounting. [[w4]]Investors replicate, hedge and modify exposures, with positions marked to market daily.
beats.finish: Module three complete. Next: arbitrage, replication, and the cost of carry.
